title: Partitioning, Sharding, Replication & Scaling
summary: One machine will eventually not be enough. Learn how databases split data across nodes (sharding) and copy it to survive failures (replication) — and what goes wrong when you do.

blocks.markdown:
When one database server can't keep up, you have two levers: **scale up** (bigger machine) or **scale out** (more machines).

- **Partitioning / sharding** splits data across multiple nodes so each holds a subset.
- **Replication** copies the same data to multiple nodes for fault tolerance and read throughput.
- These are independent techniques — most production systems use both together.
- The hard part is *consistency*: keeping replicas in sync and routing queries correctly. See [cap-consistency-base](cap-consistency-base).

blocks.subTitle: Vertical vs horizontal
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to handle more load.

| | Vertical (scale up) | Horizontal (scale out) |
|---|---|---|
| How | Bigger CPU/RAM/disk | More machines |
| Limit | Hardware ceiling | Near-infinite |
| Cost | Expensive jump | Commodity hardware |

**Vertical** is simpler and still the first move; **horizontal** is needed when one machine hits its ceiling or when you need fault tolerance.

**Partitioning** means splitting one large dataset into smaller pieces called **partitions** (or **shards**). Each shard lives on a different node and handles a subset of reads and writes.

- A **shard key** (also called partition key) is the column or hash used to decide which shard a row belongs to.
- Good shard keys spread load evenly; bad ones concentrate traffic on one shard — a **hotspot**.
- Related: [distributed-databases](distributed-databases).

- Queries that touch one shard stay local and fast.

blocks.subTitle: Range vs hash partitioning
blocks.markdown:
Two dominant strategies for assigning rows to shards.

| | Range | Hash |
|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Contiguous key ranges | hash(key) mod N |
| Range queries | Fast — hits one shard | Scatter across all |
| Hotspot risk | High (sequential inserts) | Low (uniform spread) |

**Range** suits time-series or sorted reads; **hash** suits uniform writes. Cassandra lets you combine both (partition key hashed, clustering key ranged within the partition).

blocks.subTitle: List / directory partitioning
blocks.markdown:
**List partitioning** assigns each row to a shard based on a fixed enumeration (e.g. region: `US→shard1`, `EU→shard2`, `APAC→shard3`).

- Good for **geographic locality** — EU traffic stays in the EU shard.
- Suffers when one value dominates (all writes are US → shard1 overloaded).
- **Directory partitioning** is a generalization: a lookup table maps any key to a shard — flexible, but the directory itself becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure.

blocks.subTitle: Shard key choice & hotspots
blocks.markdown:
Choosing a bad shard key is the most common sharding mistake.

- **Monotone keys** (auto-increment IDs, timestamps): every new write lands on the last shard — a write hotspot.
- **Low-cardinality keys** (boolean, 3-value status): too few distinct values → too few shards → imbalanced load.
- **Celebrity / skewed keys**: a single user_id that drives 10 % of traffic overwhelms its shard.

Fix: add a random suffix to the key (salting), or pick a composite key. Hotspot avoidance is worth more than query convenience.

blocks.subTitle: Rebalancing
blocks.markdown:
When you add or remove shards you need to move data — **rebalancing**.

- **Fixed number of partitions** (e.g. Elasticsearch): pre-split into many more partitions than nodes; adding a node steals whole partitions. Simple but wastes space upfront.
- **Dynamic partitioning** (HBase): split a shard when it grows too large, merge when it shrinks. Adapts automatically.
- **Consistent hashing**: arranges hash space in a ring; adding a node only moves the fraction of keys between it and its neighbor. Minimizes data movement.

blocks.subTitle: Why replicate
blocks.markdown:
**Replication** keeps copies of the same data on multiple nodes. Goals:

- **Fault tolerance** — if one node dies, another has the data.
- **Read throughput** — spread reads across replicas.
- **Low latency** — serve reads from the replica closest to the user.

The challenge: every write must reach all replicas, and replicas can fall behind. The degree of this lag and its effects is the core tradeoff of replication design.

blocks.subTitle: Single-leader replication
blocks.markdown:
**Single-leader** (master-slave) replication: one node accepts all writes (the **leader**); the others (**followers / replicas**) receive a log of those writes and apply them.

- Reads can go to any replica (read replicas) — great for read-heavy workloads.
- Writes always go to the leader — the leader is a bottleneck and a single point of failure for writes.
- On leader failure, a **failover** promotes a follower — risk of data loss if the new leader hadn't received the latest writes.

Used by: PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL, Kafka topic leaders.

- The gap between leader and follower is **replication lag**.

blocks.subTitle: Multi-leader & leaderless
blocks.markdown:
Two alternatives when single-leader write throughput or availability isn't enough.

- **Multi-leader** (multi-master): multiple nodes accept writes. Useful for multi-datacenter setups where each DC has its own leader. Downside: **write conflicts** when two leaders accept conflicting writes to the same row — hard to resolve correctly.
- **Leaderless** (Dynamo-style): any node accepts writes; writes and reads go to multiple nodes simultaneously using **quorums** (W + R > N). Highly available; eventual consistency; conflict resolution by last-write-wins or vector clocks.

See [cap-consistency-base](cap-consistency-base) for the consistency tradeoffs.

blocks.subTitle: Sync vs async replication
blocks.markdown:
How quickly must a follower confirm a write before the leader acknowledges it to the client?

| | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
|---|---|---|
| Durability | Strong — follower confirmed | Weak — leader may fail before follower catches up |
| Write latency | Higher | Lower |
| Availability | Lower (follower must be up) | Higher |

In practice most systems use **semi-synchronous**: one follower is synchronous, the rest async — a balance between durability and performance.

blocks.subTitle: Replication lag & consequences
blocks.markdown:
**Replication lag** is the delay between a write reaching the leader and that write appearing on a replica. Under async replication this can range from milliseconds to seconds.

Consequences:
- **Read-your-writes violated**: a user writes their own profile, then reads from a lagging replica and sees stale data.
- **Monotonic reads violated**: user refreshes a page, the second request hits a more-lagged replica and sees older data than the first.
- **Causality violations**: a reply appears before the original post.

Fix options: route a user's reads to the leader for a window after a write; use sticky sessions; use synchronous replication for critical paths. See [caching-performance](caching-performance).

blocks.subTitle: Choosing a shard key
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you choose a shard key?**

Pick a key that: (1) has high cardinality so data spreads across many shards, (2) distributes write traffic evenly (avoid monotone IDs or timestamps), (3) keeps related rows together so common queries touch one shard. For a social feed: `user_id` is better than `created_at`. If a celebrity user is a hotspot, add a random suffix (salting).

blocks.subTitle: Range vs hash sharding
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Range vs hash partitioning — when do you pick each?**

**Range** preserves sort order so range queries (last 7 days) hit one shard — but sequential writes create hotspots. **Hash** distributes writes evenly — but a range query must scatter to all shards. Choose range for time-series analytics; hash for uniform write workloads like user events.

blocks.subTitle: Replication topologies
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Single-leader vs multi-leader — key difference?**

Single-leader: only one node accepts writes; simple conflict model, but write throughput and availability are limited by one leader. Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes; great for multi-datacenter writes, but write conflicts are hard to resolve and easy to get wrong. Most teams stay single-leader unless they have a clear multi-DC write requirement.

**Q: What is replication lag and what can go wrong?**

Async replication delay. Risks: stale reads (read-your-writes failure), monotonic read violations, causality anomalies. Fix: route post-write reads to the leader, or use synchronous replication for critical paths.
